screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this chapter we build a clear mental model of how Linux sees storage: physical devices, logical partitions, and filesystems. You will learn to distinguish HDDs and SSDs by behavior and use case, choose the proper partitioning scheme for disk sizes and firmware, and use command-line tools to safely partition and format disks. We’ll also cover common filesystem options — ext4, XFS, and Btrfs — and explain inodes and blocks so you understand how files actually map to disk space. Throughout, I’ll call out common mistakes, like using MBR on a disk larger than two terabytes or forgetting to mkfs before mounting. By the end you’ll be able to inspect disks, pick the right tools, and prepare storage safely. Which part feels most unfamiliar to you right now?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Overview
Understanding Storage Devices and Filesystems
How disks, partitions, and filesystems work together to store and protect data

This lesson teaches the three-layer model you will use daily: device, partition table, filesystem. You will learn commands and practical checks to prepare a new disk, and avoid common mistakes that lead to data loss. Expect terminal-first demos later where we create partitions with fdisk and gdisk, then format with mkfs.

We emphasize safe workflows: identify the right device, confirm sizes with lsblk, and always double-check before writing partition tables.

Explore Key Topics
HDD vs SSD
When to favor cheaper bulk storage vs high I/O performance.
MBR vs GPT
Partition limits, redundancy, and UEFI boot requirements.
Filesystems
ext4, XFS, Btrfs — tradeoffs of stability, scalability, and features.
Concept Map
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Physical Disk
HDD or SSD: capacity, performance, durability
Partition Table
MBR vs GPT controls partition layout and boot behavior
Filesystem
ext4, XFS, Btrfs: how files, inodes, and blocks are stored
Quick Orientation
Start by identifying new devices with lsblk, choose MBR or GPT intentionally based on disk size and firmware, then use fdisk or gdisk to partition, mkfs to create filesystems, and blkid or fsck to verify.

Throughout, I’ll highlight common mistakes and verification steps so you can operate safely on production systems. These objectives set the stage for confident, repeatable storage administration tasks.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Skills
screens.narratorSegment: This second objective screen focuses on the practical command-line skills you will acquire and why they matter. You will learn to identify new disks with lsblk and fdisk -l so you never mistake the OS disk for a new one. You will practice creating partitions using fdisk for MBR and gdisk for GPT, including the gdisk 'o' command to initialize a new GPT table. You will also format partitions with the mkfs family — for example mkfs. ext4 — and verify result with blkid and fsck. The why matters: these commands change on-disk metadata; one wrong target device and you can erase production data. So we will practice the habit of printing the partition table before writing it, using small test disks in a VM, and running fsck only on unmounted filesystems. Each objective provides practice steps and a verification checkpoint. By training with safe examples, you develop muscle memory that prevents costly mistakes in real environments.

Common Mistake

screens.title: HDD vs SSD — physical differences and use cases
screens.narratorSegment: Let’s start with the physical layer: HDDs and SSDs. A Hard Disk Drive uses spinning platters and a mechanical read/write head. This makes it cost-effective per gigabyte and suitable for large archives, backups, and bulk storage where sequential throughput matters more than latency. An SSD uses flash memory with no moving parts; it gives much lower latency and higher input and output operations per second, which benefits operating systems, databases, and applications that perform many small random reads and writes. A concrete example: use an HDD for cold backup storage where access is infrequent, and use an SSD for the root filesystem or a database volume where fast random input and output reduces query latency. A common misconception is that SSDs always outperform HDDs in every workload. For very large sequential transfers and raw cost per terabyte, HDDs can still win. Another contrast is durability: SSDs handle shock better but have write endurance limits — choose appropriate enterprise-grade SSDs for heavy write workloads. Takeaway: match device type to workload by examining access patterns, capacity needs, and budget. Ask yourself: is my workload latency-sensitive or archival? That question guides the choice.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › HDD vs SSD
Short definition
HDD: mechanical, spinning platters. SSD: solid-state flash memory without moving parts. Each has tradeoffs in speed, cost, and durability.
Use case: HDD
Large archives, backups, and cold storage where cost per gigabyte matters more than latency.
Use case: SSD
Operating systems, databases, and I/O-bound applications that benefit from low latency and high random IOPS.
Key Takeaway
Choose by access pattern: random small I/O favors SSD; large sequential writes and cost constraints favor HDD.
Concrete example
# Example allocation
# Web server: root filesystem on SSD for fast boot and low latency
# Backup archive: mounted on HDD for large capacity and lower cost
Common misconception
Believing SSDs always provide a net benefit. Some archival workloads with very large sequential transfer needs still favor HDDs for cost reasons.

screens.title: Partitions — logical divisions of a disk
screens.narratorSegment: A partition is a logical slice of a physical disk that lets you treat different regions independently. Think of a partition as a container: it has a start and end sector and appears to the OS as a separate device node like /dev/sdb1. There are practical reasons to partition: separate the OS from user data, isolate swap space, or host multiple filesystems with different mount options. For example, putting /var on its own partition prevents runaway log growth from filling the root filesystem. Partitions also enable different filesystems on the same disk — you can use ext4 for one partition and XFS for another. A common misconception is that every partition must be the same size or type; in reality sizes reflect needs. Another important point is that partitions are governed by the partition table (MBR or GPT). Creating a partition does not place a filesystem on it — it only creates a defined area. After partitioning, you must create a filesystem inside the partition before mounting and using it. Takeaway: partition thoughtfully to contain failures and manage space, and remember to format partitions before use.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Partitions
What is a partition?
A logical section of a disk defined by a partition table. It appears as a separate block device node and must be formatted before use.
Why partition?
  • Separate system and user data to limit accidental full disks.
  • Assign different filesystems or mount options to different workloads.
  • Reserve swap or special-purpose partitions.
Concrete scenario
You add a 2TB disk to a server. Create /dev/sdb1 as a 1.9TB partition for data and /dev/sdb2 as a 100GB partition for snapshots. Format each partition appropriately before mounting.
Mistake to avoid
Assuming a partition implies a filesystem. You still need to run mkfs on the partition node before mounting.

screens.title: MBR vs GPT — partitioning schemes compared
screens.narratorSegment: Now compare partition schemes. MBR is the older Master Boot Record standard that stores its partition table at the start of the disk. It has two main limitations: a maximum usable disk size of about two terabytes and a maximum of four primary partitions unless you use an extended partition and logical partitions inside it. GPT — the GUID Partition Table — was designed to overcome these constraints. GPT supports disks much larger than 2TB, allows many more partitions (Linux commonly uses a 128 partition default), and stores redundant copies of the partition table across the disk for improved robustness. GPT is also required for UEFI booting on modern systems. A practical example: choose GPT for a new 4TB drive so you can use the full capacity and enjoy redundancy. A common misconception is that MBR is always simpler; while its table is simpler, MBR is unsuitable for modern large disks. Another substantive point: gdisk can warn you if an MBR table already exists and offers an option to create a new GPT table — use this intentionally and not by accident. Final takeaway: pick GPT for modern large disks and UEFI systems; use MBR only for legacy compatibility when size and partition count are not a concern.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › MBR vs GPT
MBR — Quick facts
  • Stores partition table at start of disk.
  • Limit: ~2TB maximum usable size.
  • Up to four primary partitions (or three primary + extended).
Use only for legacy compatibility
GPT — Quick facts
  • Supports very large disks and many partitions.
  • Stores redundant partition tables for robustness.
  • Required for UEFI booting on modern machines.
Preferred for modern systems
Concrete decision rule
If disk > 2TB or system uses UEFI, choose GPT. For small legacy disks with strict compatibility needs, MBR can be acceptable.

screens.title: Using fdisk to create an MBR partition
screens.narratorSegment: Here we run through a typical fdisk session to create an MBR partition. First, identify the device with lsblk or sudo fdisk -l and confirm its name — you do not want to edit your OS disk by mistake. With a safe test disk, run sudo fdisk /dev/sdb. Inside fdisk you use n to create a new partition, p for primary, choose the partition number, accept defaults for the first sector if you want it at the start, and specify size such as +1G for a one-gigabyte partition. Use p to print the partition table and verify settings. When satisfied, w writes changes and exits. A concrete example: creating /dev/sdb1 and then running sudo mkfs. ext4 /dev/sdb1 to format it. A common misconception is that pressing w is reversible; once written, changes update the on-disk table and can remove existing data. Always double-check the printed table and the device path. Closing question: before you press w, what three checks will you perform to ensure safety? Using fdisk to create an MBR partition means identify device, create partition with n, verify with p, and write with w — always confirm device names first.. In practical terms, interactive terminal-style walkthrough of an fdisk session. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › fdisk — MBR Partitioning
Terminal demo (read-only)
$ sudo fdisk /dev/sdb
Command (m for help): n
Partition type
   p   primary (1 primary, 0 extended, 3 free)
   e   extended
Select (default p): p
Partition number (1-4, default 1): 1
First sector (2048-41943039, default 2048): [Enter]
Last sector, +/-sectors or +/-size{K,M,G} (2048-41943039, default 41943039): +1G
Command (m for help): p

Example shows creating a 1GB primary partition and writing the table. Replace /dev/sdb with your actual test disk.
Explanation & tips

  • w: write changes to disk — this is the point of no return for on-disk table changes.
Check before write
Confirm device path, partition start/end, and that the partition numbering matches your plan.

screens.title: Using gdisk to create a GPT partition table
screens.narratorSegment: gdisk is the GPT-aware equivalent of fdisk. Use it when you need GPT features such as support for disks larger than two terabytes or redundant partition table copies. Start by confirming device identity with lsblk. Then run sudo gdisk /dev/sdb on your target disk. If an MBR table exists you may see warnings; this is expected when transitioning or demonstrating both schemes. To initialize a new empty GPT table, use the o command and confirm with y. Then create a new partition with n, accept defaults or specify sizes like +500M, print the table with p, and write changes with w. A concrete example: run o to clear previous tables when preparing a clean GPT disk, then n to create /dev/sdb1 of 500MB for testing. Common misconception: assuming gdisk will automatically preserve an existing MBR layout — it warns you and lets you decide. Takeaway: use gdisk when GPT is required, and deliberately initialize or convert tables with care. Using gdisk to create a GPT partition table means gdisk provides gpt-specific commands; use 'o' to create a new gpt table and 'n' to add partitions, verifying before write.. In practical terms, initialize gpt, create partitions, and handle existing mbr warnings. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › gdisk — GPT Partitioning
Terminal demo (read-only)
$ sudo gdisk /dev/sdb
Command (? for help): o
This option deletes all partitions and creates a new protective GPT table. Proceed? (Y/N): y
Command (? for help): n
Partition number (1-128, default 1): [Enter]
First sector (34-..., default = 2048) : [Enter]
Last sector (2048-..., default = ...) : +500M
Command (? for help): p
Command (? for help): w
Final checks complete. About to write GPT data. Proceed? (Y/N): y
Note: gdisk warns about existing MBR tables; use o only when you intend to create a new GPT layout.
Tips & precautions
  • gdisk's o command creates a clean GPT table — confirm you want to remove existing partition metadata.
  • GPT redundancy stores partition tables in multiple locations for recovery; this adds robustness.
  • After writing, verify partitions with lsblk and blkid before creating filesystems.
Pro Tip
Use small test disks in VMs when practicing gdisk commands to avoid accidental data loss on production hardware.

screens.title: Creating filesystems with mkfs
screens.narratorSegment: After partitioning, you must create a filesystem so the OS can store files and metadata. The mkfs command family provides specific frontends like mkfs. ext4, mkfs. xfs, and mkfs. btrfs. For example, run sudo mkfs. ext4 /dev/sdb1 to create an ext4 filesystem on the first partition. ext4 is a stable general-purpose journaling filesystem, XFS is optimized for large files and scalability, and Btrfs adds copy-on-write, snapshots, and checksums for data integrity. A concrete example: after creating /dev/sdb1 with fdisk, run sudo mkfs. ext4 /dev/sdb1 and then sudo blkid /dev/sdb1 to confirm that TYPE="ext4". Important misconception to avoid: formatting a partition erases existing data — do not mkfs on a partition you intend to keep. Also, some filesystems require specific mount options or utilities to maintain advanced features; learn the appropriate admin tools for the filesystem you choose. Final takeaway: mkfs turns a partition into a usable filesystem; pick the filesystem that aligns with performance, scaling, or feature needs. Creating filesystems with mkfs means use mkfs.ext4, mkfs.xfs, or mkfs.btrfs to create filesystems; verify with blkid and understand feature tradeoffs before formatting.. In practical terms, format a partition so it can store files. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › mkfs — Create Filesystems
Command examples
# Create ext4 on partition
sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1

# Create XFS on partition
sudo mkfs.xfs /dev/sdb2

# Create Btrfs on partition
sudo mkfs.btrfs /dev/sdb3
After running mkfs, use sudo blkid /dev/sdb1 to confirm TYPE and UUID.
Choosing a filesystem
  • ext4: robust default, broad compatibility.
  • XFS: high performance for large files and parallel I/O.
  • Btrfs: snapshots, checksums, copy-on-write for advanced features.
Danger
Formatting erases data. Never mkfs on a device containing data you need to keep.

screens.title: Inodes and blocks — how files map to disk
screens.narratorSegment: Filesystems manage data using two central concepts: inodes and data blocks. An inode is the metadata record for a file or directory. It stores ownership, permissions, timestamps, size, and pointers to the data blocks that hold the file’s content. Data blocks are fixed-size chunks of disk space where the actual bytes live. When you create a file, the filesystem allocates an inode number and assigns data blocks as needed. For example, a small file may fit in a handful of blocks; a large file will use many blocks and potentially indirect pointers from the inode. A typical misconception is to equate filenames with inodes. Filenames live in directory entries that map a name to an inode number — the inode is the authoritative record. Another practical point: inode exhaustion can prevent creating new files even if disk space remains, so for workloads that create many small files, plan filesystem parameters accordingly. Takeaway: inodes track metadata and block pointers; blocks store content. Knowing this helps with troubleshooting low-file errors and planning for file quantity versus file size. Inodes and blocks — how files map to disk means every file has an inode that points to data blocks. understand both to plan for many small files or very large files.. In practical terms, understanding file metadata and data allocation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Inodes & Blocks
Inodes explained
An inode stores a file's metadata and pointers to its data blocks. Filenames are directory entries mapping names to inode numbers.
Why it matters
If a filesystem runs out of inodes you cannot create new files even when space remains. Tune inode counts for workloads with many small files.
Blocks explained
Blocks are fixed-size units where content is stored. Files use one or more blocks; larger files use indirect block pointers from the inode.
Concrete example
A filesystem with 4KB blocks storing a 1KB file still consumes one 4KB block. Many small files raise block overhead.
Key Takeaway
Understand both inode and block constraints when planning for file counts, performance, and diagnostic troubleshooting.

screens.title: Verifying filesystems: fsck, blkid and wipefs
screens.narratorSegment: Verification and repair are essential parts of filesystem administration. blkid is a quick way to inspect a device and confirm the filesystem TYPE and UUID after formatting — for example sudo blkid /dev/sdb1 should show TYPE="ext4". fsck is the filesystem check and repair utility. Use fsck to check for and repair filesystem inconsistencies; however, only run fsck on unmounted filesystems to avoid corruption. For example, sudo fsck -f /dev/sdb1 forces a check on an ext4 filesystem. wipefs removes filesystem signatures from a device, which is useful when you want to clear traces before reinitializing a disk — for example sudo wipefs -a /dev/sdb. A common mistake is running fsck on a mounted root filesystem without appropriate maintenance mode; this risks damage. Another pitfall is assuming blkid will always show meaningful data on an uninitialized partition; it will show nothing if no filesystem exists. Takeaway: verify filesystem identity with blkid, repair with fsck on unmounted devices, and use wipefs carefully when deliberately clearing metadata. Verifying filesystems: fsck, blkid and wipefs means use blkid to confirm type, fsck for repairs on unmounted filesystems, and wipefs only when you intend to clear signatures.. In practical terms, check, identify, and clean filesystems safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Verify & Repair
Common commands
# Identify filesystem type
sudo blkid /dev/sdb1

# Force check (unmounted)
sudo fsck -f /dev/sdb1

# Remove filesystem signatures (destructive)
sudo wipefs -a /dev/sdb
Always unmount or use maintenance mode before running fsck on a live system.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Running fsck on a mounted filesystem that is actively being used.
  • Using wipefs -a on a disk that contains partitions you need to preserve.
  • Assuming blkid will show TYPE if no filesystem exists — it will not.
Key Takeaway
Confirm identity with blkid, repair safely with fsck on unmounted devices, and clear metadata with wipefs only when intentional.

screens.title: Lab walkthrough: preparing a new virtual disk
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough follows the hands-on scenario in the chapter. Start by adding a new virtual disk of at least two gigabytes to your VM and reboot so the OS sees it. Identify the disk with lsblk or sudo fdisk -l and note its device node, for example /dev/sdb. First, practice partitioning with fdisk for MBR: sudo fdisk /dev/sdb, create a 1GB primary partition using n and +1G, print with p, and write with w. Next, if you want to explore GPT, run sudo gdisk /dev/sdb, use o to make a new empty GPT table (confirm), then n to create a 500MB partition and w to write. After partition creation, format with sudo mkfs. ext4 /dev/sdb1. Verify with sudo blkid /dev/sdb1 to confirm TYPE="ext4". If you need to clean the disk for repeated testing, use sudo wipefs -a /dev/sdb, which removes signatures. Remember: always confirm device names and run fsck only on unmounted partitions. A common trap is reusing the wrong device — double-check lsblk output before any destructive command. This procedure gives you safe practice and reproducible checks to prepare new storage.

Step-by-step commands
# Identify new disk
lsblk

# MBR partition with fdisk
sudo fdisk /dev/sdb
# inside: n p 1 [Enter] +1G p w

# GPT partition with gdisk
sudo gdisk /dev/sdb
# inside: o n [Enter] +500M p w

screens.title: ext4, XFS, and Btrfs — filesystem tradeoffs
screens.narratorSegment: Linux offers multiple filesystem choices, each with tradeoffs. ext4 is a mature and stable journaling filesystem suitable as a general-purpose default. It balances performance and reliability and is widely supported across distributions. XFS excels on large files and high parallel input and output — it's often chosen for enterprise data volumes where scalability and online growth matter. Btrfs provides advanced features like copy-on-write, snapshots, checksums for data and metadata, and built-in RAID capabilities; it is feature-rich for workloads that need snapshots and integrity checks but can be more complex to manage. A concrete decision example: run ext4 for your VM root disk for compatibility and safety, choose XFS for a large video repository with huge files, and consider Btrfs for systems where snapshotting and checksumming are operational requirements. A common misunderstanding is that a newer filesystem automatically replaces older ones; compatibility, tooling maturity, and backup strategies still make ext4 and XFS sensible choices in many deployments. Final takeaway: pick the filesystem that matches your operational needs, and test resize or snapshot workflows before deploying critical data. ext4, XFS, and Btrfs — filesystem tradeoffs means ext4 for stability, xfs for large-scale and parallel i/o, btrfs for snapshots and checksums — test before production use.. In practical terms, selecting a filesystem based on features and workload. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

ext4
Default, journaling, robust, broad compatibility. Good default for system and general data volumes.
XFS
High performance for large files and scalable throughput. Often used for enterprise and large-volume storage.
Btrfs
Copy-on-write, snapshots, checksums, and built-in RAID features. Powerful but more complex to manage.
Concrete selection rule
Use ext4 for general-purpose and compatibility, XFS where large-file throughput matters, and Btrfs when snapshots, checksums, or built-in pooling are essential.

screens.title: Avoiding the most common mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: This slide covers the mistakes most likely to cause data loss and how to prevent them. First, always verify the device node: confirm with lsblk and note sizes and existing mount points. A frequent error is targeting /dev/sda (the OS disk) instead of the intended /dev/sdb. Second, remember that partitioning alone does not create a filesystem — forgetting mkfs leads to mount failures reported as unknown filesystem type. After creating partitions, run mkfs. ext4 or the appropriate mkfs.* command to format the partition. Third, never run fsck on a mounted filesystem unless you understand the risk and are in a maintenance state where the filesystem is read-only or unmounted; otherwise fsck can cause corruption. Fourth, when using gdisk to convert tables, heed warnings about existing MBR data and use the o command only when you intend to create a new GPT table. A final tip: practice workflows in a VM with disposable disks, and make a checklist: identify, print partition table, confirm, write, format, verify. Ask yourself: which check on that list will you automate with a script and which will you keep manual for safety?

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this chapter we build a clear mental model of how Linux sees storage: physical devices, logical partitions, and filesystems. You will learn to distinguish HDDs and SSDs by behavior and use case, choose the proper partitioning scheme for disk sizes and firmware, and use command-line tools to safely partition and format disks. We’ll also cover common filesystem options — ext4, XFS, and Btrfs — and explain inodes and blocks so you understand how files actually map to disk space. Practical commands you will see include lsblk, fdisk, gdisk, mkfs, blkid, and fsck. Knowing these lets you prepare new storage for databases, archives, or system volumes without accidentally overwriting the wrong disk. A typical practical workflow is: identify the device, create a partition table appropriate for your disk, add partitions, create a filesystem, then verify and mount. Throughout, I’ll call out common mistakes, like using MBR on a disk larger than two terabytes or forgetting to mkfs before mounting. By the end you’ll be able to inspect disks, pick the right tools, and prepare storage safely. Which part feels most unfamiliar to you right now?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify physical storage types and pick the right device for the workload, explain how partition tables create logical sections of a disk, and select MBR or GPT based on disk size and boot requirements. You will also be able to create partitions with fdisk and gdisk, create a filesystem using mkfs, and verify it with blkid and fsck. Each objective pairs a practical skill with its impact: for example, choosing GPT for disks larger than two terabytes avoids wasted capacity; formatting a partition before mounting prevents mount failures. We’ll practice a hands-on scenario where you add a virtual disk, partition it both ways for demonstration, and format an ext4 filesystem, so the concepts move from theory to command-line skill. Throughout, I’ll highlight common mistakes and verification steps so you can operate safely on production systems. These objectives set the stage for confident, repeatable storage administration tasks.

This second objective screen focuses on the practical command-line skills you will acquire and why they matter. You will learn to identify new disks with lsblk and fdisk -l so you never mistake the OS disk for a new one. You will practice creating partitions using fdisk for MBR and gdisk for GPT, including the gdisk 'o' command to initialize a new GPT table. You will also format partitions with the mkfs family — for example mkfs. ext4 — and verify result with blkid and fsck. The why matters: these commands change on-disk metadata; one wrong target device and you can erase production data. So we will practice the habit of printing the partition table before writing it, using small test disks in a VM, and running fsck only on unmounted filesystems. Each objective provides practice steps and a verification checkpoint. By training with safe examples, you develop muscle memory that prevents costly mistakes in real environments.

Let’s start with the physical layer: HDDs and SSDs. A Hard Disk Drive uses spinning platters and a mechanical read/write head. This makes it cost-effective per gigabyte and suitable for large archives, backups, and bulk storage where sequential throughput matters more than latency. An SSD uses flash memory with no moving parts; it gives much lower latency and higher input and output operations per second, which benefits operating systems, databases, and applications that perform many small random reads and writes. A concrete example: use an HDD for cold backup storage where access is infrequent, and use an SSD for the root filesystem or a database volume where fast random input and output reduces query latency. A common misconception is that SSDs always outperform HDDs in every workload. For very large sequential transfers and raw cost per terabyte, HDDs can still win. Another contrast is durability: SSDs handle shock better but have write endurance limits — choose appropriate enterprise-grade SSDs for heavy write workloads. Takeaway: match device type to workload by examining access patterns, capacity needs, and budget. Ask yourself: is my workload latency-sensitive or archival? That question guides the choice.

A partition is a logical slice of a physical disk that lets you treat different regions independently. Think of a partition as a container: it has a start and end sector and appears to the OS as a separate device node like /dev/sdb1. There are practical reasons to partition: separate the OS from user data, isolate swap space, or host multiple filesystems with different mount options. For example, putting /var on its own partition prevents runaway log growth from filling the root filesystem. Partitions also enable different filesystems on the same disk — you can use ext4 for one partition and XFS for another. A common misconception is that every partition must be the same size or type; in reality sizes reflect needs. Another important point is that partitions are governed by the partition table (MBR or GPT). Creating a partition does not place a filesystem on it — it only creates a defined area. After partitioning, you must create a filesystem inside the partition before mounting and using it. Takeaway: partition thoughtfully to contain failures and manage space, and remember to format partitions before use.

Now compare partition schemes. MBR is the older Master Boot Record standard that stores its partition table at the start of the disk. It has two main limitations: a maximum usable disk size of about two terabytes and a maximum of four primary partitions unless you use an extended partition and logical partitions inside it. GPT — the GUID Partition Table — was designed to overcome these constraints. GPT supports disks much larger than 2TB, allows many more partitions (Linux commonly uses a 128 partition default), and stores redundant copies of the partition table across the disk for improved robustness. GPT is also required for UEFI booting on modern systems. A practical example: choose GPT for a new 4TB drive so you can use the full capacity and enjoy redundancy. A common misconception is that MBR is always simpler; while its table is simpler, MBR is unsuitable for modern large disks. Another substantive point: gdisk can warn you if an MBR table already exists and offers an option to create a new GPT table — use this intentionally and not by accident. Final takeaway: pick GPT for modern large disks and UEFI systems; use MBR only for legacy compatibility when size and partition count are not a concern.

Here we run through a typical fdisk session to create an MBR partition. First, identify the device with lsblk or sudo fdisk -l and confirm its name — you do not want to edit your OS disk by mistake. With a safe test disk, run sudo fdisk /dev/sdb. Inside fdisk you use n to create a new partition, p for primary, choose the partition number, accept defaults for the first sector if you want it at the start, and specify size such as +1G for a one-gigabyte partition. Use p to print the partition table and verify settings. When satisfied, w writes changes and exits. A concrete example: creating /dev/sdb1 and then running sudo mkfs. ext4 /dev/sdb1 to format it. A common misconception is that pressing w is reversible; once written, changes update the on-disk table and can remove existing data. Always double-check the printed table and the device path. Closing question: before you press w, what three checks will you perform to ensure safety? Using fdisk to create an MBR partition means identify device, create partition with n, verify with p, and write with w — always confirm device names first.. In practical terms, interactive terminal-style walkthrough of an fdisk session. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

gdisk is the GPT-aware equivalent of fdisk. Use it when you need GPT features such as support for disks larger than two terabytes or redundant partition table copies. Start by confirming device identity with lsblk. Then run sudo gdisk /dev/sdb on your target disk. If an MBR table exists you may see warnings; this is expected when transitioning or demonstrating both schemes. To initialize a new empty GPT table, use the o command and confirm with y. After partitioning, you must create a filesystem so the OS can store files and metadata. The mkfs command family provides specific frontends like mkfs. ext4, mkfs. xfs, and mkfs. btrfs. For example, run sudo mkfs. ext4 /dev/sdb1 to create an ext4 filesystem on the first partition. ext4 is a stable general-purpose journaling filesystem, XFS is optimized for large files and scalability, and Btrfs adds copy-on-write, snapshots, and checksums for data integrity. A concrete example: after creating /dev/sdb1 with fdisk, run sudo mkfs. ext4 /dev/sdb1 and then sudo blkid /dev/sdb1 to confirm that TYPE="ext4". Filesystems manage data using two central concepts: inodes and data blocks. An inode is the metadata record for a file or directory. It stores ownership, permissions, timestamps, size, and pointers to the data blocks that hold the file’s content. Data blocks are fixed-size chunks of disk space where the actual bytes live. When you create a file, the filesystem allocates an inode number and assigns data blocks as needed. For example, a small file may fit in a handful of blocks; a large file will use many blocks and potentially indirect pointers from the inode. A typical misconception is to equate filenames with inodes. Filenames live in directory entries that map a name to an inode number — the inode is the authoritative record. Another practical point: inode exhaustion can prevent creating new files even if disk space remains, so for workloads that create many small files, plan filesystem parameters accordingly. Takeaway: inodes track metadata and block pointers; blocks store content. Knowing this helps with troubleshooting low-file errors and planning for file quantity versus file size. Inodes and blocks — how files map to disk means every file has an inode that points to data blocks. understand both to plan for many small files or very large files.. In practical terms, understanding file metadata and data allocation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Verification and repair are essential parts of filesystem administration. blkid is a quick way to inspect a device and confirm the filesystem TYPE and UUID after formatting — for example sudo blkid /dev/sdb1 should show TYPE="ext4". fsck is the filesystem check and repair utility. Use fsck to check for and repair filesystem inconsistencies; however, only run fsck on unmounted filesystems to avoid corruption. For example, sudo fsck -f /dev/sdb1 forces a check on an ext4 filesystem. wipefs removes filesystem signatures from a device, which is useful when you want to clear traces before reinitializing a disk — for example sudo wipefs -a /dev/sdb. A common mistake is running fsck on a mounted root filesystem without appropriate maintenance mode; this risks damage. Another pitfall is assuming blkid will always show meaningful data on an uninitialized partition; it will show nothing if no filesystem exists. Takeaway: verify filesystem identity with blkid, repair with fsck on unmounted devices, and use wipefs carefully when deliberately clearing metadata. Verifying filesystems: fsck, blkid and wipefs means use blkid to confirm type, fsck for repairs on unmounted filesystems, and wipefs only when you intend to clear signatures.. Linux offers multiple filesystem choices, each with tradeoffs. ext4 is a mature and stable journaling filesystem suitable as a general-purpose default. It balances performance and reliability and is widely supported across distributions. XFS excels on large files and high parallel input and output — it's often chosen for enterprise data volumes where scalability and online growth matter. Btrfs provides advanced features like copy-on-write, snapshots, checksums for data and metadata, and built-in RAID capabilities; it is feature-rich for workloads that need snapshots and integrity checks but can be more complex to manage. A concrete decision example: run ext4 for your VM root disk for compatibility and safety, choose XFS for a large video repository with huge files, and consider Btrfs for systems where snapshotting and checksumming are operational requirements. A common misunderstanding is that a newer filesystem automatically replaces older ones; compatibility, tooling maturity, and backup strategies still make ext4 and XFS sensible choices in many deployments. Final takeaway: pick the filesystem that matches your operational needs, and test resize or snapshot workflows before deploying critical data. ext4, XFS, and Btrfs — filesystem tradeoffs means ext4 for stability, xfs for large-scale and parallel i/o, btrfs for snapshots and checksums — test before production use.. This slide covers the mistakes most likely to cause data loss and how to prevent them. First, always verify the device node: confirm with lsblk and note sizes and existing mount points. A frequent error is targeting /dev/sda (the OS disk) instead of the intended /dev/sdb. Second, remember that partitioning alone does not create a filesystem — forgetting mkfs leads to mount failures reported as unknown filesystem type. After creating partitions, run mkfs. ext4 or the appropriate mkfs.* command to format the partition. Third, never run fsck on a mounted filesystem unless you understand the risk and are in a maintenance state where the filesystem is read-only or unmounted; otherwise fsck can cause corruption. Fourth, when using gdisk to convert tables, heed warnings about existing MBR data and use the o command only when you intend to create a new GPT table. A final tip: practice workflows in a VM with disposable disks, and make a checklist: identify, print partition table, confirm, write, format, verify. Ask yourself: which check on that list will you automate with a script and which will you keep manual for safety?

These three concept cards summarize essentials to carry forward. First, match device type to workload: SSDs for low-latency and high IOPS; HDDs for large, cost-sensitive capacity. Third, partitioning only defines containers — you must create a filesystem with mkfs before mounting; forgetting this is a very common cause of 'unknown filesystem type' errors.
